epithet: Umm al-Mu'minin (Mother of the Believers); al-Siddiqah bint al-Siddiq (the Truthful, daughter of the Truthful)
role: Scholar and jurist of the Sahaba
summary: Aisha bint Abi Bakr (RA) was the daughter of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, the wife of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and one of the foremost scholars of the first generation of Islam. Through her unparalleled proximity to the Prophet ﷺ in his domestic life, she transmitted knowledge of hadith, fiqh, and the Seerah that is foundational to Islamic scholarship — earning the title al-Siddiqah bint al-Siddiq from classical scholars.
biography:
Aisha bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq al-Taymiyyah was born around 614 CE in Makkah, the daughter of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (RA) and Umm Ruman bint Amir al-Kinaniyyah. She grew up in a household devoted to Islam from her earliest memory — her father was the closest companion of the Prophet ﷺ, and she had never known a time when her family was not Muslim. The Prophet ﷺ used to visit the home of Abu Bakr frequently, and Aisha grew up hearing his conversations and seeing his character from childhood.

She married the Prophet ﷺ and came to live with him in Madinah shortly after the Hijrah. Her marriage to the Prophet ﷺ was, according to multiple narrations, a marriage informed by divine indication — the Prophet ﷺ reported that he was shown Aisha in a dream and told: 'This is your wife.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab al-Nikah). The Prophet ﷺ said of her: 'The superiority of Aisha over other women is like the superiority of tharid (a meat-and-bread dish) over other foods.' (Sahih al-Bukhari, Kitab Fada'il Ashab al-Nabi).

The domestic knowledge she acquired through years of close daily companionship with the Prophet ﷺ was of a kind no other companion could fully replicate. She observed his worship in the privacy of the night, his manner of sleeping, eating, and dress, his interactions with family and guests, and his private conversations on matters of theology, law, and personal conduct. This knowledge made her one of the primary authorities on the Prophet's Sunnah in matters that others — particularly the male Sahaba — could not have access to.

Her scholarly contribution to Islam is immense. She is the source of approximately 2,210 hadith in the major collections — the fifth-highest narrator among all the Sahaba, and the highest-ranked female narrator by far. Among the subjects on which she transmitted detailed knowledge: the Prophet's prayer at night (tahajjud), the rules of ritual purity (taharah) and specifically ghusl (major ritual bath), the manners and obligations of marriage and divorce, the Prophet's illness and death, the prayers of the nights of Ramadan, and the details of the Hajj pilgrimage. Many rulings in Islamic fiqh depend entirely on narrations from her that no other companion could have witnessed.

She was also renowned for her knowledge of Arabic poetry, genealogy, and medicine — arts that were part of the cultural inheritance of educated Qurayshi families. The companion Abu Musa al-Ash'ari (RA) said: 'Whenever a matter became obscure to us, the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, we asked Aisha (RA) and we always found knowledge with her about it.' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi, graded sahih). Her status as a faqihah (female jurist) was recognized by the major Tabi'un (Successors) who sought her opinions and transmitted her rulings.

She also corrected senior male companions when she believed they had erred in transmitting the Prophet's teachings. Al-Dhahabi and Ibn al-Qayyim each document cases in which she corrected or qualified narrations from even major Sahaba, and in most cases her corrections are accepted by later scholars of hadith as accurate.

The incident of the ifk (slander) — when she was falsely accused of impropriety during a campaign — is recorded in the Quran itself (Surah al-Nur, 24:11-20), where Allah directly declared her innocence from above the seven heavens. This event, which grieved the Prophet ﷺ and the Muslim community deeply, ended with a Quranic revelation that exonerated her in terms that classical exegetes — Ibn Kathir, al-Tabari, and al-Baghawi — describe as a divine honor granted to her uniquely among human beings.

After the Prophet's death (11 AH / 632 CE), Aisha remained in Madinah, where she taught thousands of students — male and female — from behind a veil. The great Tabi'i scholars including al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr (her nephew), Urwah ibn al-Zubayr (her nephew), and the female scholar Amrah bint Abd al-Rahman are among her primary students and transmitters.

During the first fitna, following the murder of Uthman ibn Affan (35 AH), Aisha participated in the movement that led to the Battle of the Camel (36 AH / 656 CE) near Basrah. She traveled with a force demanding justice for Uthman's murder and accountability from Ali ibn Abi Talib's government. The battle, which was fought without her direct command or intention for large-scale bloodshed, resulted in many casualties. Classical scholars — following the methodology of Ibn Taymiyyah and al-Dhahabi — hold that Aisha and the companions with her were engaged in ijtihad on a complex political matter, acted with sincere conviction, and that none are to be condemned. After the battle, Ali (RA) treated Aisha with full honor and respect, and she returned to Madinah, where she continued teaching for over two more decades.

She died on the seventeenth night of Ramadan, 58 AH (678 CE), at approximately sixty-six years of age. She was buried in the Baqi cemetery in Madinah at her own request — declining to be buried in her chamber beside the Prophet ﷺ out of a sense of unworthiness for that specific honor she attributed to the later wives. The Prophet ﷺ had said to her during his final illness: 'O Aisha, this is Gabriel who greets you with peace.' She replied: 'And upon him be peace. You see what I cannot see' — a narration recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari that classical scholars cite as evidence of her exceptional spiritual station.

key_events.event: Born in Makkah to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Umm Ruman
Emigrated to Madinah with the Hijrah; came to live with the Prophet ﷺ
Incident of the ifk (slander) — acquitted by direct Quranic revelation (Surah al-Nur 24:11-20)
Accompanied the Prophet ﷺ on the Farewell Hajj
The Prophet ﷺ died with his head in her lap in her chamber
Participated in the Battle of the Camel near Basrah
Returned to Madinah after the battle; resumed teaching
Died in Madinah on the 17th of Ramadan; buried in al-Baqi

notable_traits: Foremost female scholar of the Sahaba — her hadith narrations are foundational to Islamic law
Gifted memory and intelligence from childhood
Rare combination of intimate domestic knowledge and rigorous scholarly discipline
Courage in correction — corrected senior Sahaba when she believed they had erred
Eloquence and skill in Arabic poetry and language
